1984.title: Nineteen Eighty-Four — Wikipedia
1984.summary: Nineteen Eighty-Four (also published as 1984) is a 1949 dystopian novel by English writer George Orwell. Set in the superstate Oceania, it follows Winston Smith, a low-ranking Outer Party member who secretly rebels against the omnipresent surveillance and propaganda of the Party led by Big Brother. Central themes include totalitarianism, mass surveillance, historical revisionism, and the manipulation of language through Newspeak. The novel introduced the English lexicon to terms such as 'Big Brother', 'doublethink', 'thoughtcrime', and '2 + 2 = 5'.

On an otherwise unremarkable Tuesday, Vernon notices strangely dressed people in cloaks whispering about 'the Potters' and a boy called Harry. That evening Albus Dumbledore and Professor McGonagall — in her cat form — wait outside 4 Privet Drive. project hail mary.title: Project Hail Mary — Wikipedia
project hail mary.summary: Project Hail Mary is a 2021 science fiction novel by Andy Weir. The story follows Ryland Grace, a middle-school science teacher who wakes up alone on a spacecraft with no memory of how he got there. He gradually recalls that he is the sole conscious crew member of a desperate one-way mission to save Earth from an astrophage — a microorganism that is dimming the Sun. The novel is told largely through alternating chapters of present-day events aboard the ship and flashback memories of the mission's planning on Earth.

project hail mary chapter 1 summary.summary: Chapter 1 opens in media res: the narrator wakes up in an unfamiliar room, connected to medical equipment, with no memory of who he is or how he got there. Two other crew members lie dead in their bunks. Through a series of basic self-tests — blinking, speaking, counting — he slowly reconstructs his identity as Ryland Grace. He explores the spacecraft, noting its alien design and the absence of windows. The chapter is written entirely in first-person present tense, reflecting Grace's amnesiac perspective. Key themes introduced: isolation, self-reliance, and the unsettling gap between competence (Grace can intuitively operate the ship) and memory (he cannot recall why he is there).

Drawing on 12 years of ethnographic fieldwork across Polynesian, Micronesian, and Melanesian communities, she develops the first unified typology of communicative silence in the Pacific literature.'

the cartography of silence.title: Review: The Cartography of Silence — Journal of Linguistic Anthropology
the cartography of silence.summary: Review in the Journal of Linguistic Anthropology (Vol. 30, No. 1, 2020): 'Tāwhiri's monograph is an essential contribution to the study of non-verbal communication in Pacific cultures. Her six-category typology of silence — ranging from *nooanoa* (held relational silence) to *faka'apa'apa* (respectful deferential silence) — is rigorously grounded in fieldwork and elegantly theorized. The opening chapter's ethnographic vignette from Fakarava is among the most compelling openings in Pacific anthropology in recent memory.' Rated essential reading.

The Cartography of Silence (Oceanic University Press, 2019) is her first monograph; her forthcoming work examines gesture systems in Micronesian navigation traditions.

ama owusu author.title: Ama Owusu — Interview, Brittle Paper
ama owusu author.summary: Brittle Paper interview (April 2023): 'I grew up near a glass workshop in Kumasi. There was a man there who made vessels for storing palm wine — nothing decorative, purely functional. But the way light moved through them in the afternoon was extraordinary. That's where the novel began.' Owusu discusses her approach to multigenerational structure, the challenge of writing Accra, and what she wanted Meridian Glass to do that contemporary African fiction hasn't done.
